The Hobbit: Bilbo Baggins, a comfortable and adventure-averse hobbit, is swept into a quest when the wizard Gandalf and thirteen dwarves arrive at his door. Together they set out to reclaim the dwarves' homeland and treasure from the fearsome dragon Smaug. Along the way Bilbo discovers unexpected courage, resourcefulness, and a strange ring with mysterious powers. The journey is full of trolls, goblins, giant spiders, and unlikely friendships forged in danger. By the end, the timid hobbit returns home changed, having proven that small people can do great things.
The Lord of the Rings: A sweeping epic about the hobbit Frodo Baggins, who inherits a powerful ring that must be destroyed before the Dark Lord Sauron can use it to conquer Middle-earth. Frodo sets out with a fellowship of humans, elves, dwarves, and hobbits, facing war, betrayal, and despair along the way. The story is as much about friendship and sacrifice as it is about battles and armies. Each member of the fellowship is tested and must find their own courage. It is ultimately a tale of how ordinary beings can carry the fate of the world.
Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone: Eleven-year-old Harry Potter discovers he is a wizard and is whisked away to Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. There he makes lifelong friends, learns magic, and uncovers the truth about his parents' deaths at the hands of the dark wizard Voldemort. The story blends humor, wonder, and mystery as Harry and his friends investigate a hidden magical stone hidden within the school. Themes of friendship, courage, and belonging run throughout. It marks the beginning of Harry's journey from an unwanted orphan to a hero of the wizarding world.
Pride and Prejudice: Elizabeth Bennet navigates the strict social expectations of Regency England while sparring with the proud and wealthy Mr. Darcy. Their initial dislike slowly gives way to mutual respect and love, but only after both must overcome their own pride and prejudice. The novel is a sharp, witty look at marriage, class, and reputation in nineteenth-century society. Austen's dialogue crackles with irony as she skewers social pretension. At its heart, it is a story about learning to see other people, and oneself, clearly.
To Kill a Mockingbird: Set in a small Southern American town during the 1930s, the novel follows young Scout Finch as her father, lawyer Atticus Finch, defends a Black man falsely accused of a crime. Through Scout's eyes, the story examines racism, injustice, and moral courage in a deeply divided community. Atticus becomes a model of quiet integrity, teaching his children to stand up for what is right even when it is unpopular. The book blends childhood innocence with harsh social realities. It remains a powerful meditation on empathy and justice.
Brave New World: In a future society engineered for stability and pleasure, humans are grown in laboratories and conditioned from birth to accept their assigned roles. Citizens are kept docile through a drug called soma and a culture of constant, shallow entertainment. When an outsider raised beyond the World State's control arrives, he exposes the emptiness beneath the society's manufactured happiness. The novel questions what freedom and individuality mean when comfort and control are offered in their place. It stands alongside 1984 as a foundational warning about dystopian futures, though its danger is pleasure rather than pain.
The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe: Four siblings step through an old wardrobe into the magical land of Narnia, a world frozen in eternal winter under the rule of the White Witch. There they meet Aslan, a great and noble lion, and become swept up in a battle between good and evil. The children must find courage and loyalty to each other as they fight to free Narnia. The story is full of talking animals, mythical creatures, and a sense of wonder at every turn. It is ultimately a tale of sacrifice, redemption, and the triumph of hope over despair.
All Quiet on the Western Front: A young German soldier named Paul Baumer volunteers for World War I filled with patriotic idealism, only to find the reality of trench warfare brutal and dehumanizing. The novel follows Paul and his classmates as they lose their innocence, their friends, and eventually their connection to the world they left behind. It offers an unflinching account of fear, camaraderie, and loss on the battlefield. Remarque strips away any glory from war, showing instead its senseless waste of young lives. It remains one of the most powerful anti-war novels ever written.
The Little Prince: A pilot stranded in the desert meets a small prince who has traveled from a tiny asteroid, visiting strange planets and odd grown-ups along the way. Through simple, poetic conversations, the little prince shares his love for a single rose he left behind and reflects on what truly matters in life. The story is a gentle critique of adult preoccupation with numbers, status, and seriousness. Its central theme is that the most important things in life are invisible to the eye and can only be seen with the heart. It remains a beloved fable about friendship, love, and loss.
Dune: On the desert planet Arrakis, young Paul Atreides is thrust into a web of political betrayal, prophecy, and interstellar power struggles over the galaxy's most valuable resource, the spice melange. After his family is betrayed, Paul must survive among the planet's fierce native Fremen and come to terms with his own destiny as a possible messianic figure. The novel weaves together ecology, religion, and politics into an epic tale of power and manipulation. It explores how prophecy and belief can be used to control entire populations. Dune is widely considered one of the greatest science fiction novels ever written.
The Alchemist: Santiago, a young Andalusian shepherd, dreams repeatedly of a treasure hidden near the Egyptian pyramids and sets out on a journey to find it. Along the way he meets a king, an alchemist, and a caravan crossing the desert, each teaching him something about listening to his heart and following what he calls his Personal Legend. The novel is a simple, parable-like story about destiny, self-discovery, and the courage to pursue one's dreams. It suggests that the universe conspires to help those who truly know what they want. It has become a modern classic about finding meaning and purpose in life.
The Kite Runner: In Kabul, Afghanistan, Amir and his servant's son Hassan share a close friendship shadowed by class and ethnic divisions, until a betrayal on the day of a kite-flying tournament shatters their bond. Decades later, now living in America, Amir is given a chance to atone for his childhood cowardice. The novel moves between the innocence of childhood friendship and the brutal realities of war and displacement in Afghanistan. It is a story about guilt, redemption, and the long shadow the past casts over a life. Themes of loyalty and forgiveness run through every page.
Fahrenheit 451: Fahrenheit 451 by Ray Bradbury is a classic dystopian novel set in a future society where books are banned and firefighters are responsible for burning them instead of putting out fires. The story follows Guy Montag, a firefighter who begins to question the oppressive system after meeting people who challenge his beliefs. As he discovers the value of books, knowledge, and independent thinking, Montag embarks on a dangerous journey in search of truth and freedom. The novel explores themes such as censorship, government control, technology, conformity, intellectual freedom, and the importance of preserving knowledge.
Romeo and Juliet:
Romeo and Juliet is a famous tragedy written by William Shakespeare. The story takes place in Verona, Italy, where two important families, the Montagues and the Capulets, are enemies.

Romeo Montague meets Juliet Capulet at a party organized by her family. Even though they come from rival families, they immediately fall in love. They decide to get married in secret, hoping that their love might bring peace between their families. Friar Laurence agrees to help them and performs the marriage.

However, the conflict between the families continues. Juliet's cousin, Tybalt, fights Romeo's friend Mercutio and kills him. Angry and upset, Romeo kills Tybalt. As punishment, Romeo is banished from Verona and has to leave Juliet.

Meanwhile, Juliet's parents want her to marry another man, Paris. Juliet refuses because she is already married to Romeo. Friar Laurence creates a plan to help them. Juliet drinks a potion that makes her appear dead for a short time. The plan is for Romeo to find her after she wakes up so they can escape together.

Unfortunately, Romeo does not receive the message explaining the plan. When he hears that Juliet is dead, he believes it is true. He returns to Verona, goes to Juliet's tomb, and drinks poison. Romeo dies next to her. Soon after, Juliet wakes up and discovers Romeo's body. Heartbroken, she kills herself with Romeo's dagger.

After their deaths, the Montague and Capulet families finally understand how destructive their hatred has been. They decide to end their conflict and make peace. The play shows that hatred and violence can have tragic consequences, while love can be powerful enough to overcome social divisions.
